extracted.intended_audience: GCC policymakers, IP legislators, IP office officials, legal drafters, and advisors on IP law reform
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended standards for reforming and harmonizing intellectual property laws and enforcement practices across GCC member states, using EU best practices and international treaties as benchmarks. Covers copyright, related rights, databases, technological protection measures, enforcement and treaty accession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design IP systems to balance welfare and dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: IP protection systems should be designed “in a manner conducive to social and economic welfare, and to a balance of rights and obligations” (TRIPS objectives and principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws should balance rewarding creativity and disseminating knowledge rather than only increasing protection; read TRIPS provisions in light of their object and purpose (Doha Declaration). Avoid adopting provisions that are 'alien' to the population or do not respond to market needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align national laws with TRIPS minimum standards
rubrics_metrics.description: GCC IP legislation should be at least in line with the TRIPS Agreement covering Copyright, Related Rights, Trademarks, Industrial Designs, Patents, Geographical Indications and Undisclosed Information (Trade Secrets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TRIPS places IP in a world trade context and obliges effective enforcement procedures and non-discrimination rules (NT and MFN). Use TRIPS as baseline when drafting or amending laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect national treatment (NT) and most-favoured-nation (MFN) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure laws and practice comply with TRIPS non-discrimination rules: national treatment (treat nationals and foreigners according to TRIPS meaning) and MFN (grant advantages to all WTO Members).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NT is reflected in most GCC IP laws though MFN is often not properly reflected and sometimes replaced by reciprocal treatment; even if not in law, both principles should be respected in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition must respond to market needs and local context
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid transposing international IP provisions that do not respond to market needs or are alien to the concerned population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful implementation depends on acceptance by affected sectors; adapt international norms to the country's socio-economic needs and capacities rather than verbatim transposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure transparency and public consultation in law-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt rules of good governance and transparency such as publishing draft laws and collecting public comments (example: SAIP practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public consultation and feedback (with agency responses) fosters societal acceptance and facilitates implementation of new IP rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure IP system effectiveness by adoption and enforcement capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The efficiency of an IP system is measured not by the level of protection in laws but by acceptance/adoption by the population and national authorities' capacity to enforce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed measures should be within the country's operating systems and aligned to human resources, legal and technical capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go beyond TRIPS for digital environment protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright laws need updates beyond TRIPS especially for protection in the digital environment (technological protection measures, rights management information, ISP liability, online content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use EU directives (e.g., Directive 2019/790, Regulation 2017/1128) and WIPO internet treaties (WCT, WPPT) as models for online content-sharing, fair remuneration, portability, and digital-era protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the three-step test for copyright exceptions/limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations and exceptions to exclusive copyright rights should conform to the three-step test in Article 13 of TRIPS: confined to special cases, not conflict with normal exploitation, and not unreasonably prejudice legitimate interests of the right holder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some GCC states (Kuwait, Oman) make exceptions subject to the three-step test; others follow Berne/TRIPS without explicit reference. Prefer explicit three-step test compliance for legal certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect moral rights and extend protection where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide moral rights protections (e.g., Article 6bis of Berne) and consider more extensive moral rights as GCC countries currently do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many GCC laws already provide for moral rights and extend protection beyond TRIPS requirements; maintain and clarify these protections in reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt resale right (droit de suite) for authors of original works
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider introduction of a resale right to benefit authors of original works of art (optional under Berne and TRIPS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saudi Arabia currently provides such right; the EC Directive 2001/84/EC can serve as model; this can be pursued regionally through a unified law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear protection for computer programs and software
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright law should explicitly protect computer programs and databases when their arrangement or selection is creative; include rules on reproduction, rental, and prohibited acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some GCC laws reflect EU Directive 2009/24/EC standards. Complement with provisions on decompilation/interoperability and clarify allowed acts (e.g., lawful preservation/replacement, adaptation in limited circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify ownership of works created in employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify whether works created by employees in the course of duties belong to the employer or the worker and under which conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GCC laws vary: some vest economic rights to employers when created in course of duties or by instruction; others preserve worker rights unless agreed otherwise. Ensure written agreements clarify ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce sui generis database protection for non-original databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider protection for databases and collections that lack originality but represent substantial investment (financial, human resources) via a sui generis right as in Directive 96/9/EC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sui generis protection grants transferrable economic rights to prohibit extraction/reuse for 15 years from creation; exceptions allowed if legitimate interests not unreasonably harmed. Use EU analyses/evaluations when designing regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect technological protection measures (TPMs) and rights management information (RMI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibit circumvention of effective TPMs and alteration/removal of RMI; criminalize manufacture/import/distribution of circumvention devices and tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All GCC countries provide varying TPM/RMI protections; laws should align with WCT/WPPT. Examples across GCC list specific prohibited acts and sanctions—adopt clear prohibitions and enforcement measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate ISP liability for online infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover the liability of internet service providers in copyright laws to address online infringement and intermediary responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Currently only Bahrain and Oman have extensive ISP liability provisions (reflecting FTA obligations); other states should consider legislating clear intermediary liability rules consistent with international practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonize IP laws regionally using international/EU models
rubrics_metrics.description: GCC countries should coordinate harmonization of digital-content related laws and can rely on EU experience and directives as guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Directive 2019/790 (digital single market), Regulation 2017/1128 (portability), and other EU instruments as starting points for regional alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain a balanced copyright term policy (caution on 70 years)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully consider whether to extend general copyright term from 50 years p.m.a. to 70 years; extension may benefit rights-holders but harm public domain and consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EU/US extended to 70 years; recommendation here is not to extend immediately so GCC public domain remains strong. Note differences between member states may complicate future unified law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accede to international IP treaties to strengthen protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Join relevant WIPO treaties (WCT, WPPT, Beijing Treaty) and other international conventions to modernize protections for performers and rights-holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bahrain, Qatar, UAE already party to some treaties; recommend Kuwait and others join the Beijing Treaty to improve performers' protection, particularly for online uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve enforcement procedures and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess and enhance procedures/practices of judges, police and customs to increase effectiveness of IP enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 6 will provide recommendations; enforcement capacity—training, procedures, institutional coordination—is crucial for effective protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalize trafficking and specific infringing acts with proportional sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibit and penalize trafficking in counterfeit labels, unauthorized reproduction/loading/renting of software, distribution of counterfeit documentation/packaging, and removal/alteration of rights management information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GCC laws contain specific prohibitions and fines (e.g., UAE fines for unauthorized use of programs). Ensure statutes specify prohibited acts and align sanctions with deterrence and proportionality.
